function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

**Java – an overview** | Topic | Details | |-------|---------| | **What it is** | Java is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible. It was originally developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle Corporation) and released in 1995. | | **Key design goals** | • *Write once, run anywhere* (WORA): compiled bytecode runs on any device equipped with a Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
• Platform independence via JVM abstraction.
• Strong memory safety and automatic garbage collection.
• Robust security model (sandboxed execution, permission checks).
• Rich standard library (java.lang.*, java.util.*, etc.). | | **Core concepts** | - **Classes & Objects:** Encapsulation of state (fields) and behavior (methods).
- **Inheritance & Polymorphism:** Reuse code through super/subclass relationships.
- **Interfaces & Abstract Classes:** Define contracts without concrete implementations.
- **Exception Handling:** Checked vs unchecked exceptions, try/catch/finally blocks.
- **Generics:** Type-safe collections and APIs.
- **Annotations:** Metadata for compile-time processing or runtime reflection. | | **Execution flow** | Source → `javac` compiler → `.class` files containing bytecode → JVM interprets/just‑in‑time compiles bytecode into native machine instructions per platform. | | **Typical use cases** | • Enterprise back‑end services (Spring Boot, Jakarta EE)
• Android mobile apps (though Kotlin now dominates)
• Desktop GUI applications (Swing, JavaFX)
• Big‑data frameworks (Apache Hadoop, Spark’s Java API)
• Embedded systems / IoT devices
• Cloud microservices, RESTful APIs, gRPC servers | | **Ecosystem** | • Build tools: Maven, Gradle, Ant
• Testing frameworks: JUnit, TestNG, Mockito
• IDEs: IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, NetBeans
• Libraries/APIs: Apache Commons, Guava, Jackson, Lombok, Spring Framework, Hibernate ORM | | **Version evolution** | Since Java SE 8 (2014), major releases occur roughly annually (e.g., Java 9 introduced modules, Java 11 LTS added new APIs, Java 17 LTS includes sealed classes, pattern matching enhancements, etc.). | | **Why still popular?** | Mature ecosystem, strong backward compatibility guarantees, extensive community support, proven performance for large-scale distributed systems, and continuous innovation (Project Loom, Project Valhalla, etc.) | --- ### Quick “Hello World” example ```java public class HelloWorld { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, world!"); } } ``` Compile: ```bash $ javac HelloWorld.java # produces HelloWorld.class ``` Run: ```bash $ java HelloWorld # prints: Hello, world! ``` That simple program demonstrates: 1. Class declaration (`public class HelloWorld`) 2. Static entry point method (`main`) required by the JVM 3. Standard output using `System.out`. Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper dives—whether it's advanced topics like concurrency primitives, module system intricacies, best practices for building production-grade services, or how Java compares to other languages!
